summary: Describes the problem of source-address-dependent routing from a host's view, covering hosts with multiple interfaces or addresses. It shows example networks to explain why source address selection and next-hop choice matter. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If different roads only allow cars from different towns, you must choose the right road for your plate. This explains why computers need to think about that.

questions: multihomed ipv6 host source address selection
subtitle: Why computers with multiple networks must choose which source address to use

tldr.problem: Hosts with multiple network interfaces or addresses face a routing problem: they must choose which source address to use and which network to send packets through, or packets will be blocked by ingress filtering.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC catalogs real network scenarios (datacenters, homes with two ISPs, phones with WiFi and cellular, corporate VPNs) and explains why both source address selection and source-dependent routing are needed.
tldr.outcome: The document provides the problem analysis that shaped RFC 8028, which became the IETF consensus on host multihoming. It guides operators and implementers on network provisioning.

facts.value: BCP 38 (RFC 2827) recommends dropping packets with spoofed sources

today: RFC 8043 is an Informational RFC that remains relevant as IPv6 adoption grows and multihomed networks become common. It is not obsoleted. RFC 8028 built on this analysis and became the IETF's recommended approach to host multihoming. The problem space described here—homes with multiple ISPs, phones with WiFi and cellular, corporate VPN overlays—continues to be a practical concern for operators and implementers.

sections.title: The Ingress Filtering Problem
sections.content:
Networks apply ingress filtering (BCP 38, RFC 2827) to block packets with fake source addresses. When a router sees a packet with a source address from outside its own networks, it drops it as potential spoofing. This works well when each host has one address, but breaks for multihomed hosts.

A host receiving multiple prefixes from multiple network providers (like a home router connected to both DSL and 4G, or a phone with WiFi and cellular) gets multiple source addresses. When it sends a packet with the wrong source address for the chosen path, the packet gets dropped by ingress filters. RFC 3704 (BCP 84) recommends that multihomed networks enforce source-address-dependent routing to prevent this, meaning routers must consider source addresses when choosing next hops.
sections.plainLanguage: Guards at each road check if you're from the right town before letting you pass. If you pick the wrong town-name for your current road, you are stuck.

sections.title: Scenarios and Their Complexity
sections.content:
The RFC describes four increasing levels of complexity:

Multi-prefix multihoming: A host has a single interface but receives prefixes from two providers. The host must select the right source address for each packet so it reaches the correct provider. The router handles source-dependent routing automatically. Example: a home with DSL and cable internet sharing one WiFi network.

Multi-prefix multi-interface: A host has two interfaces, each connected to a different provider's router, each providing a different prefix. Now the host must both select the correct source address AND choose which interface to send through. Both decisions are linked: choose the wrong source address or wrong interface, and the packet gets dropped. Example: a laptop with both Ethernet and WiFi, connected to different networks.

Home networks: A home router (CPE) with two internet connections serves hosts inside the home network. Each CPE broadcasts its own prefix. Internal hosts must choose which CPE to route through and which source prefix to use, or pick the wrong combination and lose connectivity.

Service-specific egress routing: Some services require specific source prefixes. A VoIP service might only accept packets from its assigned address range. A host must select both the correct service address and the correct next hop that reaches that service.
sections.plainLanguage: Start simple: pick the right address-town. Then harder: pick the right address-town AND the right interface-road. Then: operate a home network. Then: different services need different addresses.

sections.title: Analysis: How Hosts Make These Choices
sections.content:
In basic multihoming (multi-prefix multihoming), the host performs source address selection (choosing which of its addresses to use) while the upstream router performs source-dependent routing (choosing which path to send the packet on). No special host routing is needed.

In multi-prefix multi-interface scenarios, the host must do both. It receives multiple prefixes from different routers on different interfaces, usually via Router Advertisements (RAs). The host needs to know which source prefixes each upstream router will accept. One approach: configure the host with explicit source address prefixes for each next hop. Another: use ICMPv6 Redirect messages from routers to steer traffic, but Redirects can only convey destination address, not source address, creating confusion.

Home networks should use source-address-dependent routing at the routers, but hosts still need proper source address selection. This requires hosts to learn which source prefixes each CPE supports, typically via Router Advertisements advertising both destination routes and acceptable source prefixes.

Provisioning Domains (PvDs) offer a solution: a consistent set of network configuration information grouped together. Explicit PvDs carry identity and configuration information via DHCP or RA options. A host can associate configuration information into PvDs and use them for routing decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: The host learns from routers which addresses work on which roads, then picks the right combo for each packet.

sections.title: Solutions: Router Advertisements and Policy
sections.content:
Router Advertisement (RA) messages can carry additional options beyond simple prefix information. The Prefix Information Option (PIO) advertises which prefixes are valid on a link. The Route Information Option (RIO) advertises specific routes. Sources suggest that RAs could carry new options advertising which source address prefixes work with each next hop, helping hosts make correct decisions.

One proposal adds new RA options explicitly listing source address prefixes supported by that router. A host receiving "Router X on Interface 1 supports source prefixes A and B" and "Router Y on Interface 2 supports source prefixes C and D" can then correctly select both source and next-hop.

Another approach relies on Rule 5.5 of RFC 6724 (Default Address Selection), which already provides guidance on source address selection in multihomed hosts. RFC 8028 (updated consensus) builds on these mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers tell hosts: 'I accept packets from addresses in town A and town B, use one of those.' Then hosts pick correctly.

sections.title: Trust and Network Configuration
sections.content: Hosts must trust the information they receive from routers about which source addresses work on which paths. A malicious router advertising incorrect source prefixes could cause packets to be dropped or misrouted. Provisioning Domain information should be authenticated based on the host's policy requirements. When multihomed hosts receive provisioning information from multiple routers on different interfaces, they should verify that the PvD identity is authentic, especially when the same PvD is advertised on multiple interfaces. Hosts should not blindly trust a route advertisement from a router on one interface telling them to send traffic via a router on another interface without appropriate authentication. These concerns are particularly important in enterprise VPN scenarios where a corporate network overlaps with home or public internet access.
sections.plainLanguage: Trust only routers you are supposed to trust. Make sure a router really is what it claims to be.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content: This RFC provides the foundational problem analysis that led to RFC 8028, which documents IETF consensus on host multihoming behavior. The scenarios and challenges described here are not hypothetical: dual-ISP homes, corporate VPNs overlapping with home networks, and service-specific routing are all in deployment. As IPv6 addresses become more common, these problems grow more urgent. Understanding the source-address-dependent routing problem space helps operators design networks that work correctly, helps implementers build hosts that behave properly, and shapes standards for how routers should advertise capabilities. The document makes no specific recommendations—that is the job of RFC 8028 and related standards—but provides the shared understanding necessary for those recommendations to make sense.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of real networks have this problem. Understanding it helps everyone build things that work.
